meta.tagline: The world's largest car-free labyrinth: medina, tanneries and a thousand years of learning

pills: The world's largest car-free city centre

overview.title: Welcome to Fes
overview.intro: Fes is Morocco's spiritual and artisan capital: within the walls of Fes el-Bali, more than nine thousand lanes, donkey caravans, coppersmiths' hammers and the world's oldest university have kept the same rhythm for a millennium. Here GPS raises the white flag early — and that is not a flaw but an invitation. Get lost: every wrong turn ends at a medersa's tiled courtyard, a tannery's vats of colour, or a shop offering mint tea. Fes is unpolished, authentic and intense — if Marrakech is the stage, Fes is the library.

local_word.definition: 'Watch out, make way!': when you hear this shout behind you in the medina, step aside — a loaded donkey or handcart is coming. The thousand-year-old traffic alert of Fes's narrow lanes.

rules.title: Put getting lost on the itinerary
rules.description: In the medina's 9,400 lanes you will lose your way — so don't fear it, embrace it. The main arteries (Talaa Kebira and Talaa Seghira) always descend to the souk; walk uphill and you reach the gates. Those two are your compass.

rules.title: Don't believe 'the road is closed'
rules.description: The self-appointed guides' classic opener is 'that way is closed, I'll take you' — the road is almost never closed. A polite but firm 'la, shukran' and keep walking; if you want a real guide, ask your riad for an official one.

rules.title: Haggling is a game — play it seriously
rules.description: In the souk the first price is an opening line: start at a third, proceed with a smile, accept the tea. Don't open a long negotiation over something you won't buy — even the game has its manners.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: ~30 min to the medina by taxi

quick_facts.label: In the medina
quick_facts.sub: No cars — loads travel by donkey

quick_facts.label: Language
quick_facts.sub: English growing on the tourist trail

tip.label: The Fes philosophy
tip.text: In Fes make a rhythm, not a schedule: medersas and souk in the morning cool, rest in the riad courtyard at noon, tea on the terraces in the late afternoon, dinner after the call to prayer. The city has run on this rhythm for a thousand years — whoever adapts, wins.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: The medina is walked — there is no other way; outside it, the little red taxis and the railway station await.

items.title: Airport to the medina
items.description: Half an hour by taxi: fix the price before boarding or have your riad arrange a transfer — it's normal for the driver to drop you at the nearest gate and describe the walk; cars do not enter the medina.

items.title: The medina — the world's largest pedestrian zone
items.description: In Fes el-Bali your only vehicle is your feet: uphill, stony and narrow. Comfortable shoes, light luggage and the 'Balak!' reflex — all three essential. Always give way to the pack donkeys and handcarts.

items.title: Petit taxi — the little red ones
items.description: Between the medina gates, the Ville Nouvelle and the Merenid tombs, take the red taxis: ask for the meter, and if it 'doesn't work', fix the price first. Cheap and practical for short distances.

items.title: Intercity by train
items.description: Fes station is in the Ville Nouvelle: Meknes in half an hour, Rabat in three, Tangier in four. Moroccan trains are comfortable and punctual — for Chefchaouen you need the CTM bus or a grand taxi.

items.title: The pack donkeys — the medina's trucks
items.description: Everything from gas bottles to bolts of leather travels by donkey and mule: this is not folklore but a working logistics system. If you want a photo, ask the owner — most will pose them with a smile.

callout.label: Direction tip
callout.text: When lost in the medina, don't wrestle with your phone: walk downhill — all main lanes descend to the souk core around the Kairaouine. From there, finding Talaa Kebira is finding home.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Fes, lodging is not a decision but an experience: a riad courtyard inside the medina, or modern comfort outside it?

local_word.definition: The traditional Moroccan house built around an inner courtyard: a blind wall to the street, and inside, a tiled court, a fountain and an orange tree. Fes's riads are the city's best secret — step through the door and the lane's chaos ends, and calm begins.

items.name: Fes el-Bali — around the Talaa
items.description: Riad rooms in the medina's heart: souk, medersas and terraces at your doorstep. A porter carries your case from the gate — the classic for those who want to wake inside the labyrinth.

items.name: Batha and around Bab Boujloud
items.description: Just inside and outside the blue gate: one step to the medina, two to a taxi. Riads and small hotels with easy access — for those who want the labyrinth in measured doses.

items.name: Ziat and the southern medina
items.description: The district of large garden riads away from the souk's density: birdsong, quiet terraces and the smell of the neighbourhood oven. For seekers of calm inside the medina.

items.name: Fes el-Jdid
items.description: The district of the royal palace and the old Jewish quarter, the Mellah: between the two medinas, low on tourists. A base for opening Fes's layers one by one.

items.name: Ville Nouvelle
items.description: The French-era new town of boulevards: hotels with big rooms, cafés and the railway station. For those who take the medina in daytime doses and return to modern comfort at night.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Fes is an inland city: spring and autumn are gold, summer a test of heat, winter cool and quiet.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The Golden Balance
items.subtitle: Spring · Mild days, orange blossom
items.description: The best season for the medina: mild days, cool evenings, orange blossom in the riad courtyards. At spring's end the sacred music festival turns the city into a world stage.

callout.label: May tip
callout.text: If you coincide with the Fes Festival of World Sacred Music (usually May-June), build the plan around it: concerts at palace gates and in historic gardens — the city's soul takes the stage.

items.label: Summer
items.name: The Heat Test
items.subtitle: Summer · Noons approaching 40 degrees
items.description: The inland heat is serious: the medina slows at midday and life moves to morning and evening. Choose a riad with a pool, set the programme early — low prices are the consolation.

callout.label: August note
callout.text: In summer, 11 to 4 is the hour of shade and courtyards: do the medersas and tannery between 8 and 10, rest in the riad at noon, live on the terraces at night. Water bottle and hat are not negotiable.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Harvest and Light
items.subtitle: Autumn · Soft sun, olive season
items.description: The heat breaks, the light turns into photographer's light, and the olive harvest begins in the surrounding villages. October is Fes's most balanced month — reasonable crowds, reasonable weather.

callout.label: October tip
callout.text: In October climb to the Merenid tombs forty minutes before sunset: the whole medina turns to gold at your feet, and the calls to prayer echo from the hills. This is Fes's best single frame.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Cool and True
items.subtitle: Winter · Cold nights, tourist-free lanes
items.description: Sunny and cool by day, cold at night — riads are stone, so ask about good heating. The tourists thin out and the medina returns to its everyday self: the most authentic season for watching the artisans.

callout.label: January tip
callout.text: Winter is exactly the time for the hammam: the scrub-and-soap ritual at a local bathhouse both warms you and lets you into Fes's daily life. Ask your riad — everyone knows the neighbourhood hammam's hours.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Fes is counted the capital of Moroccan cooking: refinement descended from palace kitchens lives on the same lane as the warmth of the medina ovens.

local_word.definition: Fava bean soup: olive oil and cumin on top, bread alongside — the medina breakfast classic that fills you for a handful of dirhams. Drunk shoulder to shoulder with locals at the morning stall.

items.name: Pastilla — the sweet-savoury crown
items.description: Pigeon or chicken with almonds and cinnamon between fine pastry leaves, icing sugar on top: the masterpiece of Fes palace cooking. The sweet-or-savoury debate ends at the first fork — it's both.

items.name: Tagine and Friday's seven-vegetable couscous
items.description: Meats slow-cooked under the conical lid, and the seven-vegetable couscous of Fridays: every riad has its own recipe. Find couscous on a Friday noon and the tradition has been honoured.

items.name: Harira and the medina breakfast
items.description: Chickpea-and-lentil harira soup with dates and chebakia pastry: Ramadan's star, on the stalls all year. With bissara it forms the medina's morning duo.

items.name: Neighbourhood oven bread — khobz
items.description: Dough kneaded at home is baked at the communal oven (ferran): the children carrying bread trays through the lanes are this system's couriers. Buying hot khobz at the oven door is allowed — ask, smile, take.
items.tag: Hot from the ferran · the neighbourhood system

items.name: Mint tea and terrace dusk
items.description: 'Moroccan whisky' is poured from a height, and the foam is a point of honour: the official drink of haggling, hospitality and terraces. Drink it at sunset over the medina — state your sugar level at the start.
items.tag: On a terrace · poured from a height

items.name: Souk grills and olive stalls
items.description: Kefta skewer smoke, charred peppers and a hundred kinds of olives: the souk's midday kitchen is the stall itself. The crowded stall is the fresh stall — join the locals' queue.
items.tag: Souk lunch · from the crowded stall

callout.label: The table rule
callout.text: Fes's best dinners are cooked not in restaurants but in riads: order tonight's dinner from your host in the morning — home-made tagine beats the souk menu every time. Bottled water over tap, and the 'cooked and hot' rule for street food.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees the tannery; these six are Fes's deeper layers.

items.name: The Merenid Tombs hill
items.description: From the ruined tombs on the northern hill the whole medina appears in one glance: minarets, terraces and the echo of the evening call to prayer. Go up before sunset and come down as the lights turn on — the shortest way to understand Fes.

items.rarity: The peak of tile and cedar
items.name: The Al-Attarine Medersa
items.description: The 14th-century medersa at the spice souk's gate: its zellij tilework, carved plaster and cedar wood are craftsmanship's summit. Smaller than Bou Inania and usually calm — stand long in its courtyard.

items.name: The Nejjarine Fondouk
items.description: The old caravanserai has become a museum of wooden arts: its three-storey courtyard is a masterwork in itself, and the roof terrace opens over the souk. The tiled fountain outside is one of the medina's most photogenic corners.

items.rarity: A green breath inside the walls
items.name: The Jnan Sbil Gardens
items.description: The century-old garden between the two medinas: palms, pools and bamboo shade. The cure for medina intensity — exit towards Bab Boujloud and you reach the blue gate through a green corridor.

items.name: The Ain Nokbi pottery workshops
items.description: In the workshop district outside the walls, Fes-blue ceramics are still shaped by hand and the zellij masters chip each tessera one by one. Less known than the tannery, and it shows the craft closer up.

items.name: Around the Kairaouine and its doorways
items.description: The heart of the world's oldest university is closed to non-Muslims, but through the doorways around it you glimpse courtyards, parts of the restored library and the air of learning that seeps into the souk. In Fes, even a doorway is a view.

callout.label: Tannery tip
callout.text: The Chouara tannery is viewed from the leather shops' terraces: the sprig of mint pressed into your hand genuinely works against the smell. The terrace is 'free' but the sales pitch comes on the way out — looking is allowed, buying is not obligatory; a polite 'la, shukran' suffices.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Fes's traps are social, not physical: a few memorised sentences disarm all the games.

items.name: The false guide and the 'road is closed' game
items.description: The 'helpful' figure who appears at the medina gates declares the way closed, walks you in circles and finally asks for a tip or a shop commission.
items.instead: Look like you know your route, say 'la, shukran' and walk. If you want a guide, have your riad book an officially badged one — price upfront, scope clear.

items.name: The sales squeeze on the tannery terrace
items.description: Up on the 'free view' terrace a jacket gets draped over you, and on the way out the heavy haggling begins.
items.instead: Say 'just looking' from the start, and give a small terrace tip willingly if you wish. If you're buying leather, the haggling is your game anyway — if not, walk down without hesitation.

items.name: The meterless taxi tour
items.description: Some taxis waiting at the medina gates 'forget' the meter; a short hop turns into the tourist tariff.
items.instead: Say 'compteur, afak' (the meter, please); if it stays off, get out and take the next one. Ask your riad the standard gate-to-gate fares in advance.

items.name: The photo-and-'gift' tip spiral
items.description: The donkey porter, the water seller, the shop front — every photo can be followed by a tip request; the bracelet handed over as a 'gift' gets invoiced later.
items.instead: Ask before photographing and treat the small tip as natural — it is a service. Politely hand back the 'gift' pressed into your palm; a smile + 'la, shukran' is this city's magic key.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Fes, saying 'la, shukran' (no, thank you) with a smile while continuing to walk is the antidote to every tourist game. It isn't rude — it's part of the rules, and everyone understands.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: A thousand-year labyrinth from blue gate to tannery

steps.title: In through Bab Boujloud
steps.description: A bissara breakfast before the blue gate, then down Talaa Kebira into the medina: as the shops open, the lane is at its truest.

steps.title: The medersa round
steps.description: Bou Inania's courtyard, then Al-Attarine's tiled silence: look closely at the zellij, plaster and cedar work.

steps.title: Nejjarine and the souk core
steps.description: Climb the fondouk museum's floors and photograph the tiled fountain; get lost among the spice and copper souks — an ear out for the Balak calls.

steps.title: A souk lunch
steps.description: Kefta skewers or a stall tagine, mint tea on top: the crowded stall is the fresh stall.

steps.title: The Chouara tannery
steps.description: Look down on the vats of colour from the leather terraces: take the mint sprig, take your photo, and enter the haggling only if your heart is in it.

steps.title: The Merenid sunset
steps.description: Taxi up the hill: the medina turns to gold at your feet as the calls to prayer echo. Dinner at the riad — the tagine you ordered this morning is ready.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Open the labyrinth layer by layer

steps.title: Classic Fes
steps.description: The one-day flow above: blue gate, medersas, souk, tannery, Merenid.

steps.title: Palaces and craft
steps.description: Fes el-Jdid in the morning: the royal palace gates and the Mellah's balconied lanes; a breath in the Jnan Sbil gardens at noon; the Ain Nokbi pottery workshops in the afternoon; a hammam ritual + terrace dinner at night.

steps.title: A day out, and farewell
steps.description: Choose your day trip: Roman-mosaic Volubilis + Meknes, or the blue city Chefchaouen; last souk shopping on return — a zellij plate, leather slippers, a pouch of spices. Farewell tea on the terrace.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Five words of Darija soften every gate of the medina; French stands by everywhere as backup.

items.meaning: Hello — answered with 'wa alikoum salam'; the greeting that opens doors
Thank you — 'shukran bezzef' means thanks a lot
'No, thank you' — the medina's most valuable sentence; with a smile, while walking
Goodbye — when the tea is finished, the deal closed, the door reached
